tryItExercises.title: Step 1: Make one inline style on the real portfolio
tryItExercises.prompt:
**Problem**

The inherited portfolio is plain HTML, and you need one deliberately local visual change without creating site-wide styling yet.

**Task**

In `index.html`, give only the Home-page `h1` an inline `color: #0f766e;`. Keep every other page, image, navigation item, text, and structure unchanged.
tryItExercises.hint: Make the change on the existing Home h1 itself; this first step is intentionally local.

help.concept: An inline declaration is useful here because it demonstrates a deliberately local one-element style before you build reusable CSS.
help.hint_1: Make the change on the existing Home h1 itself; this first step is intentionally local.
help.hint_2: Check Home in the preview: only the Jordan Lee heading should turn teal, while every other page and element stays unchanged.

sourceChecks.message: Add the required inline color declaration to the Home-page Jordan Lee h1.

sketchBlocks.title: Move page-level rules into a <style> block
sketchBlocks.bodyMarkdown:
When several elements on **one page** need coordinated styling, repeating `style="..."` attributes becomes noisy. An internal stylesheet moves CSS into a **`<style>` element**, normally inside the document `<head>`:

```html
<style>
  h1 {
    color: #0f766e;
  }
</style>
```

This solves an organization problem: the page's styling rules live together instead of being scattered across individual tags. It is cleaner than inline CSS for one document, but a second HTML page cannot automatically reuse those rules.

**Line by line:** First, `<style>` opens the page's internal stylesheet. Second, `h1` selects the heading. Third, the braces hold its declaration block. Fourth, `color: #0f766e;` defines the text color. Finally, `</style>` ends the internal stylesheet.

The second task refactors the same page from inline styling to an internal stylesheet without changing the visual result.

tryItExercises.title: Step 2: Refactor the same Home style into <style>
tryItExercises.prompt:
**Problem**

The heading color works, but keeping presentation inside the `h1` mixes styling with the element itself. For a page-level rule, the CSS should live together in the document head.

**Task**

Keep the same visual result, remove the inline style from the Home-page `h1`, and place `h1 { color: #0f766e; }` inside a `<style>` element in `index.html`.
tryItExercises.hint: Move the same declaration into the document head rather than changing the `color` value.

help.concept: An internal style block keeps page-level presentation together while preserving the same visual result.
help.hint_1: Move the same declaration into the document head rather than changing the `color` value.
help.hint_2: Check the preview after refactoring: the Home heading should look exactly the same, but the h1 tag should return to clean semantic HTML.

sourceChecks.message: Move the h1 color into an internal style element and remove the inline h1 style.

sketchBlocks.title: Scale the same rule into an external stylesheet
sketchBlocks.bodyMarkdown:
As a site grows, keeping CSS inside every HTML document creates duplication. An **external stylesheet** moves reusable presentation rules into a separate file such as `styles.css`, then HTML links to it:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
```

```css
h1 {
  color: #0f766e;
}
```

This separation solves the maintainability problem: multiple pages can share one visual system, and one change in `styles.css` can update every page that links to it. HTML stays focused on structure and meaning while the stylesheet carries reusable presentation.

**Line by line:** First, `<link` creates a relationship from the HTML document. Second, `rel="stylesheet"` tells the browser the linked resource contains CSS. Third, `href="styles.css"` names the stylesheet file. In `styles.css`, `h1` selects headings and the `color` declaration defines their presentation.

The third task uses both files: add the stylesheet link in `index.html`, then place the reusable rule in `styles.css`. From the next lesson onward, `styles.css` becomes the main editing surface unless a task explicitly needs an HTML class, id, stylesheet link, or inline-style change.

tryItExercises.title: Prepare the shared stylesheet rule
tryItExercises.prompt:
**Problem**

The Home page still owns its `h1` color inside an internal `<style>` block, but the portfolio is about to share one external stylesheet.

**Task**

Keep every HTML file unchanged for this step. In `styles.css`, replace the placeholder comment with `h1 { color: #0f766e; }`. The next step will connect all four pages to this prepared stylesheet.
tryItExercises.hint: Only prepare styles.css in this step; do not change the HTML links yet.

help.concept: An external stylesheet can be prepared before documents are linked to it, which avoids breaking the current visual result mid-refactor.
help.hint_2: Add the reusable h1 color rule there.

tryItExercises.title: Connect every portfolio page to the shared stylesheet
tryItExercises.prompt:
**Problem**

The reusable `h1` rule now lives in `styles.css`, but the portfolio documents are not yet using that shared file.

**Task**

Connect Home, About, and Contact with `<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">`. Connect the nested Projects page with `<link rel="stylesheet" href="../styles.css">`. On Home, remove the internal `<style>` block now that the external stylesheet owns the `h1` rule.
tryItExercises.hint: Use styles.css from the root pages and ../styles.css from projects/portfolio.html; remove Home's internal style block.

help.concept: Relative paths depend on each document's folder. Root pages and a nested project page reach the same stylesheet differently.
help.hint_1: Home, About, and Contact use href="styles.css".
help.hint_2: Projects uses href="../styles.css" and Home removes `<style>`.

quizDraft.title: Choose CSS's job
quizDraft.prompt: What is CSS primarily responsible for on a web page?
quizDraft.hint: Think about which layer changes appearance without changing the document's structural meaning.

help.concept: Web pages separate structural meaning from visual presentation.
help.hint_1: One layer describes what the content is; another controls how it looks.
help.hint_2: Choose the layer responsible for appearance rather than document structure.

quizDraft.title: Identify the stylesheet connection
quizDraft.prompt: Which pieces are part of the external stylesheet connection shown in this lesson?
quizDraft.hint: Think about the markup in the document head that describes an external resource to the browser.

help.concept: Connecting an external resource requires markup that identifies the resource relationship and its location.
help.hint_1: The browser needs to know both what kind of resource it is and where to find it.
help.hint_2: Choose every markup piece used together in the document head; ignore unrelated programming concepts.

quizDraft.title: Order the CSS feedback loop
quizDraft.prompt: Arrange the workflow from requirement to validation.
quizDraft.hint: Begin with the styling requirement and finish only after the source has been checked.

help.concept: A CSS feedback loop moves from requirement to edit, visual inspection, and validation.
help.hint_1: The browser preview belongs after the source edit.
help.hint_2: Validation is the final step after you have inspected the rendered result.

quizDraft.title: Place the stylesheet resource
quizDraft.prompt: Complete the statement about where the browser resource connection belongs.
quizDraft.hint: Think about the part of an HTML document that describes resources used by the page.

help.concept: External stylesheets are document resources referenced from the metadata area of the page.
help.hint_1: The connection is not placed inside a CSS declaration or after the document closes.
help.hint_2: Choose the document area used for metadata and external resource references.

quizDraft.template: The stylesheet resource connection belongs inside the [blank1] element.

quizDraft.title: Recognize what makes external CSS reusable
quizDraft.prompt: Which statements describe why an external stylesheet works well for this multi-page portfolio? Select all that apply.
quizDraft.hint: Think about reuse across several documents and how file location affects the path used to reach one shared stylesheet.

help.concept: External CSS separates reusable presentation from individual HTML documents.
help.hint_1: Focus on what allows several pages, including a nested page, to share one file.
help.hint_2: External CSS does not require duplicated style blocks or rewritten page content.

options: One shared CSS file can style multiple HTML pages that link to it.

quizDraft.title: Name the reusable stylesheet method
quizDraft.prompt: Complete the statement about where reusable site styling belongs.
quizDraft.hint: Think about the approach that keeps rules in a separate .css file linked by the HTML document.

help.concept: CSS can live on one element, inside one document, or in a separate reusable stylesheet file.
help.hint_1: This method lets multiple HTML documents reference the same presentation rules.
help.hint_2: Choose the method associated with a separate .css file rather than a style attribute or style element.
